articles.title: OpenAI unveils plan to protect critical services from AI cyberattacks
articles.description: OpenAI is launching a new initiaitve designed to provide subsidized access to its models to water systems, electricity providers, local governments and other critical services . Why it matters : Critical infrastructure organizations — which have long lacked the budget, manpower and time needed to shore up their cyber defenses — have been struggling to prepare for the anticipated wave of AI-enabled cyberattacks. Driving the news: OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced the new program while hosting 300 security leaders for a summit at the company's headquarters Thursday. Axios first reported on the summit and Brockman's anticipated announcement. Zoom in: OpenAI is committing $1 billion to a new Daybreak for Frontline Defenders initiative focused on protecting essential services around the world. The $1 billion will come in the form of expanded subsidized access to models, training, technical support and partnerships for participating organizations. OpenAI is also launching Daybreak for America program, which will provide access to its models to local governments, water systems, electricity providers, regional banks and other critical infrastructure. As part of Daybreak for America, OpenAI is starting a pilot program with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center to train cyber defenders at state and local governments on using their models. OpenAI is also working with more than 35 technology and cybersecurity services to embed the AI lab's advanced models into their tools, services and workflows. Threat level: For years, cyber officials have feared that AI models will soon be capable of autonomously discovering and chaining together vulnerabilities in complex systems that power public utilities and services. While frontier labs like OpenAI have largely restricted access to the advanced cyber capabilities of their most powerful models, rapid improvements in open-weight models' capabilities are raising fears that AI-enabled attacks will be here sooner than anticipated. OpenAI says the new program will allow lesser-resourced utilities to review legacy code, analyze suspicious activity, identify and validate vulnerabilities, prioritize the most serious risks and develop and test security patches. Reality check: Expanding services and training doesn't solve all of the security problems that have plagued critical infrastructure for decades — which AI-enabled tools will likely now exacerbate. Many entities also need more workers who understand the nuances of protecting the physical systems they're trying to defend from digital threats. Go deeper: AI is supercharging hacks of everyday utilities

articles.title: Todd Blanche's 'unlawful' actions to punish DOJ Attorney revealed in court filing
articles.description: Attorney General Todd Blanche unlawfully fired a career Justice Department lawyer hours after she refused to help restore actor Mel Gibson's gun rights, a lawsuit alleges. Elizabeth Oyer, who reviewed clemency requests as the department's pardon attorney until March 2025, filed the complaint Thursday in federal court in Washington, D.C. Blanche was not the attorney general when he signed her termination memo, according to the complaint. He was the deputy attorney general, the department's second-ranking official . "This removal was unlawful," the lawsuit states, arguing that the firing violated Oyer's due process rights, her protections under federal civil service law and her First Amendment right to political association. The memo accused Oyer of no misconduct and gave no reason that federal law allows for removing a career executive, the complaint says. "Pursuant to Article II of the Constitution and the laws of the United States, your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated," it read. Before being named deputy attorney general of the Justice Department, Blanche had represented President Donald Trump at his Manhattan hush-money trial and in both federal criminal cases brought by special counsel Jack Smith. Only weeks after Trump's inauguration, Oyer was placed on a working group assigned to identify people who had lost their gun rights to criminal convictions but might deserve to have them restored, the complaint says. The work was "an unusual task for the Office of the Pardon Attorney," the complaint says. Oyer took it on. Her office produced a list of about 95 people with old, nonviolent convictions who had been vetted and judged unlikely to reoffend, according to the filing. Blanche's staff cut the list to nine and asked Oyer to write a memo recommending those nine, the complaint says. "Mr. Blanche's staff then came back to Ms. Oyer with another request: they asked her to add the actor Mel Gibson to the list," the complaint says. Gibson had lost the right to own a gun after a domestic violence conviction, and he had asked the attorney general to restore it, according to the complaint. Oyer had "serious concerns about the public safety implications." "Over half of the women murdered in the United States are killed by a current or former intimate partner," says the department's own guide on domestic violence and firearms, quoted in the complaint. "The presence of firearms significantly escalates the danger in relationships where there is domestic violence by increasing the risk of homicide by 500%." Gibson had never been investigated, unlike everyone else on the list, and Oyer's staff had no way to judge whether he was likely to reoffend, the complaint says. She emailed her concerns to Blanche's staff on March 6, 2025, and said she could not recommend restoring Gibson's gun rights. "Later the same day, a senior official on Mr. Blanche's staff called Ms. Oyer and urged her to recommend reinstatement of Mr. Gibson's gun rights anyway in consideration of the fact that Mr. Gibson had a personal relationship with President Trump," the complaint says. "The official employed a bullying tone and suggested to Ms. Oyer that she would be wise to make the recommendation," the filing adds. Oyer sent a new memo the next day that declined to recommend it, saying she did not know the particulars of Gibson's case and that the decision was the attorney general's, the complaint notes. A few hours later, the complaint says a colleague pulled Oyer out of an unrelated meeting to tell her that security officers were waiting in her office with her termination papers. "Ms. Oyer returned to her office, where two DOJ security officers handed her a memo from Mr. Blanche, instructed her to pack up her personal belongings, and escorted her out of the building," the lawsuit explains. Federal law allows a career senior executive to be removed only for misconduct, neglect of duty, malfeasance, or refusing a reassignment, the complaint says. The law also requires 30 days' notice and a chance to respond. Oyer says she received neither. The lawsuit points out that the department's own position is that only the attorney general can remove a department official under Article II. It has argued in other litigation that a removal by a lower-ranking official is "void ab initio," or invalid from the start, according to a copy of that filing attached to the complaint. Pam Bondi was the attorney general in March 2025. Blanche was not, and by the department's own standard, Oyer argues, the memo that ended her 13-year career never legally removed her. The Senate confirmed Blanche as attorney general over a year after Oyer was fired. The vote was 50-49 , with two Republicans joining every Democrat in opposition. While serving as Justice Department head, Blanche worked to settle Trump's private lawsuit against the IRS on terms favorable to the president. "President Trump did not pursue his claims until he once again occupied the White House and had appointed his former lawyer ... to prominent positions in the DOJ," U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams wrote in July, voiding the IRS settlement, according to CBS News . "It is risible to suggest that there was ever adverseness between the Parties." Williams ordered copies of her ruling sent to the New York and District of Columbia bar associations for disciplinary review of Blanche, The Hill reported. "There was no collusion in this case, and the partisan judge who speculated otherwise has disregarded decades of precedent," the department said in a statement . The department has fired employees who worked on Trump-related cases since January 2025, citing the president's constitutional powers, Reuters reported. At least 37 came from Smith's team, and Blanche fired Peter Carr, the career spokesman for both Smith and former special counsel Robert Mueller, CBS News reported. Oyer spent 16 months at the Merit Systems Protection Board, which Congress created to hear federal personnel disputes, without receiving a substantive review, according to the complaint. The board dismissed her appeal in June, leaving her without a decision for at least six more months. It had already ruled in March that it lacks jurisdiction over many Article II firings, which would shut her out entirely, the complaint says. She is now in federal court. Her suit brings six counts and asks a judge to void the removal and order her reinstated. Blanche gave a different reason for the firing when he appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee in July seeking confirmation. "The decisions that she had made as pardon attorney ... were completely inconsistent with President Trump," Blanche said at the hearing , pointing to her recommendation to commute the sentences of everyone on federal death row. "I took an oath to uphold the law, not to do political favors," Oyer said in July, in a separate records lawsuit she brought against the department.

articles.title: MAGA pollster warns Republicans sleeping as red states slip from their grasp
articles.description: A MAGA pollster who called President Donald Trump's last two White House wins warned Republicans are sleeping on red states now slipping toward Democrats. In a Wednesday episode of Bulwark Takes , Rich Baris laid out the case during an interview with former GOP operative Tim Miller . Baris, the director of Big Data Poll, argued that the party is coasting on Trump's 2024 margins in states he won't be on the ballot to defend. "Republicans are going to run out of a coalition soon if they don't build on what he started to build in '24," Baris said. He pointed to a cluster of seats that the GOP treats as locked down. The Republicans' assumption is "hubris," Baris said. "They just thought Ohio and Iowa and even Texas would be within their grasp forever because of how Donald Trump performed in them," Baris said. "It's hubris. I don't know what else to call it." Republicans have "repeatedly understated Democrats' chances" in Kansas, Nebraska, and Montana, Baris said. He described those three states as a "sleeper" cluster with "longtime populist and progressive roots that aren't as red as people seem to think." Baris was blunter still about Texas, where the party redrew congressional maps off Trump's numbers. "You don't perform like Donald Trump performs in Texas, folks. I hate to tell you, you don't," Baris said. "Hispanics don't like you the way that they like Trump in 2024." He said the party built those maps "with the same arrogance," using Trump's ceiling as a floor and treating gains he called "squandered" as permanent. Cost of living will be the biggest issue for voters, Baris warned. "Socialism" attacks fall flat with voters when "you can't pay your own bills," Baris said. "They're much more afraid that they can't pay their rent or their car payment or get back-to-school clothes for their kids and fill up the refrigerator than they are about Republicans throwing around the word 'socialism,'" Baris said.

articles.title: AJK PM orders bureaucracy to gear up for 100-day reform agenda
articles.description: MUZAFFARABAD: Azad Jam­mu and Kashmir (AJK) Prime Min­ister Iftikhar Gillani on Wednesday directed the bureaucracy to gear up for implementation of the government’s 100-day reform agenda , saying his foremost priority was to introduce systemic reforms to ease the difficulties of the common man and create new opportunities. Speaking at his first meeting with government secretaries at the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, Mr Gillani said his government had come to serve the people and its performance would be visible “on the ground”. “Our foremost priority is to bring reforms to the system, create ease for the common man and generate new opportunities,” he said, adding that the government would address the challenges facing the state with the cooperation of the bureaucracy. He said the administrative mach­inery had important responsibilities in translating government policies into tangible results and stres­sed the need for collective efforts. “The success of any government largely depends on the efficiency, commitment and sense of responsibility of its administrative machinery. I expect the AJK bureaucracy to work with dedication and a sense of urgency to implement the reform agenda in letter and spirit,” he said. Mr Gillani said the government would provide all necessary support to officials to deliver meaningful reforms and improve public service delivery. He said unemployment was a major challenge in the state and announced plans to introduce a youth engagement programme and demand-based skills development programmes in the social sector. He also promised relief to people in transport and healthcare services, saying measures would be taken on a priority basis to reduce their difficulties. ‘Practical measures’ The prime minister said the government was committed to translating its reform programme into practical measures and making its impact visible to the people. He said the 100-day agenda also demonstrated the seriousness of the party’s central leadership towards AJK. Separately, the prime minister attended briefings by Chief Secretary Khushal Khan and Inspector Gen­eral of Police (IGP) retired Capt Lia­qat Ali Malik on the organisational structures of the Services and General Administration Depart­ment and the police department, respectively. The IGP also briefed the prime minister on the department’s performance and future needs, as well as the overall law and order situation in the territory. Earlier, upon his arrival at the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, Mr Gillani was received by his principal secretary and officers and staff of the secretariat. Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026
